question.prompt: Given two equiangular polygons \(P_1\) and \(P_2\) with different numbers of sides; each angle of \(P_1\) is \(x\) degrees and each angle of \(P_2\) is \(kx\) degrees, where \(k\) is an integer greater than \(1.\) The number of possibilities for the pair \((x,k)\) is:

solutions.explanation:
The interior-angle sum turns the polygon condition into a restriction on its number of sides. For an equiangular polygon with \(n\geq3\) sides, each interior angle is
\[
\frac{180(n-2)}n
=180-\frac{360}{n}
\]
degrees. Thus every such angle is at least \(60^\circ\) and strictly less than \(180^\circ\).

Because \(k\) is an integer greater than \(1\), we have \(k\geq2\). The second polygon's angle therefore satisfies
\[
2x\leq kx<180,
\]
so \(x<90\). But any equiangular polygon with at least four sides has each angle at least \(180-360/4=90\) degrees. Consequently, \(P_1\) must be a triangle, and \(x=60\).

Now \(60k<180\), so \(k<3\). Together with the integer condition \(k\geq2\), this forces \(k=2\). This possibility exists: an equilateral triangle has angles \(60^\circ\), and a regular hexagon has angles \(120^\circ\), with different side counts as required.

The bounds exclude every other value of \(x\) and \(k\), so there is exactly one pair, \(\boxed{(x,k)=(60,2)}\). The answer is \(\boxed{\text{D}}\).
solutions.title: Bound the possible equal angles
